You write Verilog practice problems for complete beginners and verify nothing yourself:
your output is checked by a simulator and by mutation testing, and any failure comes back to you.

Reply with ONE JSON object in a ```json code block and nothing else. Keys:
  "spec": plain-English problem statement, 50-150 words. Say what top_module must do and what
          each provided module does. Do NOT give the wiring: which bits go to which instance, what
          a carry-in or select is tied to, or how outputs are combined. Working that out is the
          exercise; the hints reveal it step by step. Never include code.
  "given_sv": Verilog source of every provided module, or "" if none.
  "ref_sv": "module RefModule(...)" with exactly the same ports as top_module, written
            behaviourally (for example with + and assign), never using the provided modules.
  "solution_sv": what a good learner submits: "module top_module(...)" built the intended way
                 (instantiating the provided modules), plus any module the learner must write.
  "directed": list of input assignments as integers, e.g. [{"a": 5, "b": 3}]. Cover the cases
              that expose the common mistakes (carries, sign bits, each select value).
  "hints": {"L0": one sentence naming the concept to think about,
            "L3": the wiring in words (which signals connect where), still no code}.
  "common_mistakes": 2-4 short descriptions of mistakes beginners make on this problem.

Rules: Verilog-2005 (logic is allowed). No system tasks ($display etc.), no `include, no initial
blocks in ref_sv or solution_sv. Clocked logic uses posedge clk. Port names and widths must match
the given top_module header exactly.

Problem id: module_shift
Outline: Chain three instances of the provided D flip-flop my_dff into a 3-stage shift register.
top_module header: module top_module(input clk, input d, output q);
Provided module(s): module my_dff(input clk, input d, output q)
The solution must instantiate: 3 x my_dff
This problem is clocked: clk is driven by the testbench.

{
  "spec": "Create a 3-stage shift register by chaining three D flip-flops. The top_module has a clock input clk, a data input d, and an output q. Each provided my_dff module is a positive-edge-triggered D flip-flop with clock clk, data input d, and output q. The shift register should capture the input d on each rising clock edge and shift it through three stages, so that q becomes the value that was applied to d three cycles earlier.",
  "given_sv": "module my_dff(input clk, input d, output q);\n  always_ff @(posedge clk) q <= d;\nendmodule",
  "ref_sv": "module RefModule(input clk, input d, output q);\n  logic [2:0] shift_reg;\n  always_ff @(posedge clk) shift_reg <= {shift_reg[1:0], d};\n  assign q = shift_reg[2];\nendmodule",
  "solution_sv": "module top_module(input clk, input d, output q);\n  logic q1, q2;\n  my_dff dff1 (.clk(clk), .d(d), .q(q1));\n  my_dff dff2 (.clk(clk), .d(q1), .q(q2));\n  my_dff dff3 (.clk(clk), .d(q2), .q(q));\nendmodule",
  "directed": [{"d": 1}, {"d": 0}, {"d": 1}, {"d": 1}, {"d": 0}, {"d": 1}],
  "hints": {
    "L0": "Think about how a shift register moves data through a chain of flip-flops on each clock cycle.",
    "L3": "Connect the input d to the first flip-flop's d, the first flip-flop's q to the second flip-flop's d, the second flip-flop's q to the third flip-flop's d, and the third flip-flop's q to the output q. All flip-flops share the same clk."
  },
  "common_mistakes": [
    "Forgetting to declare intermediate signals between flip-flop stages.",
    "Connecting the flip-flops in the wrong order (e.g., output of third to input of first).",
    "Using the same signal name for multiple flip-flop outputs causing contention.",
    "Not using the same clock for all flip-flops."
  ]
}
